title: English → Logic Translator
goal: Turn any English sentence, even a long one, into a formula, then pick out **every** formula that means the same. That is Quiz 2's Q3b.
magic: Neither A nor B = `¬A ∧ ¬B`. Not both = `¬(A ∧ B)`.
`¬` grabs only the next thing. Brackets decide everything else.
Find the MAIN joiner first. It splits the sentence into two halves.
One row where two formulas differ = not equivalent.

blocks.title: 💡 Learn it, one idea at a time
blocks.sub: Needs L2 first. Every idea: 🧒 picture → 🎓 official version → 👀 one worked example → ✋ your turn → 🪤 the trap.

blocks.title: The small joiners: and, but, or, not, neither…nor
blocks.picture: "I'm tired **but** I'll go." Both facts are true: I'm tired, and I'll go. *But* adds a feeling, not new logic. To logic it's just **and**.
blocks.official: *and · but · although · yet · however · `;`* → `∧`. *or* → `∨` (inclusive: both is fine). *not* → `¬`. *neither A nor B* → `¬A ∧ ¬B`. *not both A and B* → `¬(A ∧ B)`. *exactly one of A, B* → `(A ∨ B) ∧ ¬(A ∧ B)`, also written `A ⊕ B` (xor).

grid.title: Cheat table
rows: A and B · A but B · although A, B
not A · it's false that A
either A or B but not both · exactly one

watch.q: "Neither the API nor the database responds." (`a` = the API responds, `d` = the database responds)
steps: Neither … nor = not this AND not that.
Same as `¬(a ∨ d)`: "it's not true that **at least one** of them responds" (De Morgan's law).

tries.q: "It's cold but sunny."
tries.why: *But* = and.

tries.q: "You can have tea or coffee." (Both is fine.)
tries.why: In this course *or* is inclusive.
tries.letters: `t` = you have tea · `k` = you have coffee

tries.q: "The tests and the linter don't both pass."
tries.why: Not both = at most one of them passes.
tries.letters: `t` = the tests pass · `l` = the linter passes

tries.q: "Exactly one of the two lamps is on."
tries.why: At least one, but not both. Also written `a ⊕ b`.
tries.letters: `a` = lamp A is on · `b` = lamp B is on

tries.q: "It's neither raining nor windy."
tries.why: Not this AND not that.

tries.q: "Although it's late, the shop is open."
tries.why: *Although* = and.
tries.letters: `l` = it's late · `o` = the shop is open

trap.test: Neither = not this **and** not that. `¬(A ∧ B)` would still allow one of them.

blocks.magic: Neither A nor B = `¬A ∧ ¬B`. Not both = `¬(A ∧ B)`.
blocks.summary: and, but, or, not, neither…nor, not both, exactly one.

blocks.title: Who grabs first: `¬`, then `∧ ∨`, then `⇒ ⇔`
blocks.picture: In maths, `2 + 3 × 4` means `2 + (3 × 4)` because × grabs first. Logic has the same kind of rule. `¬` grabs first, and it only grabs the very next thing.
blocks.official: The lecture's order: **`¬` first → then `∧` and `∨` → then `⇒` and `⇔` last.** The slides don't rank `∧` against `∨`, so **always bracket** when you mix them. Formulas can also use `⊤` (always true) and `⊥` (always false).

tries.q: Add brackets to show how it is read: `¬a ∨ b ⇒ c`
tries.why: `¬` first, then `∨`, and `⇒` last.

tries.q: Are `¬(p ∨ q)` and `¬p ∨ q` the same? Find one row.
tries.a: **No.** Row `p = T, q = T`: `¬(p ∨ q)` = F, but `¬p ∨ q` = T.
tries.why: Where the `¬` sits changes everything.

tries.q: In `¬p ∧ q`, what does the `¬` apply to?
tries.why: `¬` grabs just the next thing. To negate everything, write `¬(p ∧ q)`.

tries.q: Why must you bracket `p ∧ q ∨ r`?
tries.a: Because `(p ∧ q) ∨ r` and `p ∧ (q ∨ r)` are different, and the slides don't say which one is meant.
tries.why: Row `p = F, r = T`: the first is T, the second is F.

tries.q: Add brackets: `p ⇒ ¬q ∧ r`
tries.why: `¬` first, then `∧`, and `⇒` last.

trap.test: `¬` never reaches past a joiner unless there's a bracket.

blocks.magic: `¬` grabs only the next thing. Brackets decide the rest.
blocks.summary: `¬` first, then `∧ ∨`, then `⇒ ⇔`, and when brackets are a must.

blocks.title: The translation recipe: find the main joiner
blocks.picture: A long sentence is like a sandwich. Find where it splits into two big halves: that word is the **main joiner**. Translate each half on its own, then join them.
blocks.official: ① Give each simple sentence a letter. Use the **positive** version: if `u` = the server is up, then "down" is `¬u`. ② Find the **main joiner**, the word that splits the whole sentence in two. ③ Translate each half. ④ Put brackets around each half.

watch.q: A lecture example. `p` = HD on the exam, `q` = you do every exercise, `r` = HD in the course. Translate (a) "You get an HD in the course **although** you don't do every exercise." (b) "To get an HD in the course you **must** get an HD on the exam."
steps: (a) The main joiner *although* = `∧`. The halves are `r` and `¬q`. So `r ∧ ¬q`.
(b) *Must* makes the exam HD **necessary**, so it goes on the right: `r ⇒ p`.

tries.q: "If the server is down or the network is slow, the page times out."
tries.why: Main joiner: *if … then*. The left half, "down or slow", is `¬u ∨ n`.
tries.letters: `u` = the server is up · `n` = the network is slow · `t` = the page times out

tries.q: "You graduate only if you pass all core courses and pay your fees."
tries.why: Main joiner: *only if*. The whole "c and f" goes on the right.
tries.letters: `g` = you graduate · `c` = you pass all core courses · `f` = you pay your fees

tries.q: "If you don't sleep, you'll be tired and grumpy."
tries.why: Main joiner: *if … then*. The right half has two parts joined by *and*.
tries.letters: `s` = you sleep · `t` = you're tired · `m` = you're grumpy

tries.q: "Access is granted if the key is valid and the token hasn't expired."
tries.why: *If* marks the left side: the whole "valid and not expired" part (🔄 order).
tries.letters: `k` = the key is valid · `x` = the token has expired · `a` = access is granted

tries.q: "We merge just in case the build passes and the review is approved."
tries.why: Main joiner: *just in case* = `⇔`. The right half is "b and r".
tries.letters: `b` = the build passes · `r` = the review is approved · `m` = we merge

trap.tempting: Translate word by word, left to right.
trap.correct: Find the main joiner first, then translate each half.
trap.test: Can you point to the one word that splits the sentence in two?

blocks.magic: Main joiner first. Halves second. Brackets always.

blocks.title: Nested conditions: *whenever … unless …*, *… provided …*
blocks.picture: "Whenever it's raining, I get wet unless I carry an umbrella." Two conditions are stacked: *whenever raining* on the outside, *unless umbrella* on the inside.
blocks.official: Translate the outer condition first, then the inner one. Two rules make the result tidy: `A ⇒ (B ⇒ C)` ≡ `(A ∧ B) ⇒ C` (**exportation**), and *C unless B* = `¬B ⇒ C`. So *whenever A, C unless B* = `A ⇒ (¬B ⇒ C)` = `(A ∧ ¬B) ⇒ C`.

watch.q: "Whenever the queue is full, new messages are dropped unless back-pressure is on." (`f` = the queue is full, `d` = new messages are dropped, `b` = back-pressure is on)
steps: Exportation: `(f ∧ ¬b) ⇒ d`. A full queue with no back-pressure → dropped.

tries.q: "The discount applies if you pay by card, provided the order is over $100."
tries.why: *Provided* is the outer if, and *if* is the inner one.
tries.letters: `o` = the order is over $100 · `c` = you pay by card · `d` = the discount applies

tries.q: "The program terminates just in case the input is positive, provided the input is an integer."
tries.why: *Provided* is the outer if. *Just in case* is the `⇔` inside it.
tries.letters: `i` = the input is an integer · `t` = the program terminates · `p` = the input is positive

tries.q: "Unless there's a storm warning, the ferry runs if it's daytime."
tries.why: Outer: unless = if not. Inner: *if it's daytime*.
tries.letters: `s` = there's a storm warning · `d` = it's daytime · `f` = the ferry runs

tries.q: Rewrite `r ⇒ (¬u ⇒ w)` with a single arrow, then with no arrow at all.
tries.a: `(r ∧ ¬u) ⇒ w`, and with no arrow: `¬r ∨ u ∨ w`.
tries.why: Exportation, then `A ⇒ B` = `¬A ∨ B` and De Morgan on `¬(r ∧ ¬u)`.
tries.letters: `r` = the job is scheduled · `u` = the upstream is healthy · `w` = a warning is logged

tries.q: Is `(a ∧ b) ⇒ c` the same as `(a ⇒ c) ∧ (b ⇒ c)`?
tries.a: **No.** Row `a = T, b = F, c = F`: the left is `F ⇒ F` = T, the right is `(T ⇒ F) ∧ …` = F.
tries.why: Needing both a and b is weaker than each of them forcing c alone.

trap.correct: `A ⇒ (B ⇒ C)` = `(A ∧ B) ⇒ C`. Moving brackets across arrows changes the meaning.
trap.test: The row A = F, B = F, C = F tells them apart.

blocks.title: Same or different? Two fast checks
blocks.picture: Two formulas are **equivalent** (`≡`) if they give the same answer in **every** row. To prove they're different you need just **one** row where they disagree, like one counterexample.
blocks.official: **Method 1, rewrite into `¬ ∧ ∨`:** `A ⇒ B` → `¬A ∨ B`. `A ⇔ B` → `(A ∧ B) ∨ (¬A ∧ ¬B)`. Push `¬` inwards with De Morgan: `¬(A ∧ B)` = `¬A ∨ ¬B` and `¬(A ∨ B)` = `¬A ∧ ¬B`. **Method 2, hunt for one row:** try the row that breaks the simpler formula. If the other formula survives that row, they're different. (Full truth tables come in L3.)

watch.q: Is `p ⇒ (q ∨ r)` the same as `(p ∧ ¬q) ⇒ r`?
steps: Method 1 on the left: `¬p ∨ q ∨ r`.
Method 1 on the right: `¬(p ∧ ¬q) ∨ r` = `¬p ∨ q ∨ r` (De Morgan).

tries.q: Rewrite `¬(p ∧ ¬q)` with no `¬` in front of a bracket.
tries.why: De Morgan: `¬(A ∧ B)` = `¬A ∨ ¬B`, and `¬¬q` = `q`.

tries.q: Is `p ⇔ q` the same as `(p ∨ ¬q) ∧ (¬p ∨ q)`?
tries.why: That's `(q ⇒ p) ∧ (p ⇒ q)` written with `∨`.

tries.q: Is `p ⇔ q` the same as `(p ∨ q) ∧ (¬p ∨ ¬q)`?
tries.a: **No.** That's "exactly one" (xor). Row `p = q = T`: `p ⇔ q` = T, the other = F.
tries.why: It says at least one AND at most one.

tries.q: Is `¬(p ⇔ q)` the same as `p ⇔ ¬q`?
tries.why: Both are true exactly when p and q differ.

tries.q: Is `(p ⇒ q) ⇒ p` the same as just `p`?
tries.why: If p = T, both are T. If p = F, the left is `T ⇒ F` = F. Same value in every row.

trap.tempting: They look alike, so they're equivalent.
trap.correct: Equivalent means the same value in **every** row.
trap.test: Hunt for one disagreeing row before you say yes.

blocks.magic: One row where they differ = not equivalent.
blocks.summary: Two fast ways to tell whether two formulas mean the same.

blocks.title: 🏋️ Practice ladder
blocks.sub: A different example every time. Think first, then reveal. Mark ✅/❌ honestly, and come back to your ❌ in 2 days.

items.q: "The pizza is hot but not cheap."
items.why: *But* = and. "Not cheap" = `¬c`.
items.letters: `h` = the pizza is hot · `c` = the pizza is cheap

items.q: "Neither email nor Slack works."
items.why: Neither–nor = not this AND not that.
items.letters: `e` = email works · `s` = Slack works

items.q: "Alice and Bob won't both come."
items.why: Not both = at most one.
items.letters: `a` = Alice comes · `b` = Bob comes

items.q: Add brackets: `¬x ∧ y ∨ z`
items.a: It can't be done safely: it's either `((¬x) ∧ y) ∨ z` or `(¬x) ∧ (y ∨ z)`, and they differ.
items.why: Only `¬` is certain, since it grabs `x` alone. The slides don't rank `∧` against `∨`, so whoever writes it must add the brackets.

items.q: "It's hot, yet the fan is off."
items.why: *Yet* = and.
items.letters: `h` = it's hot · `f` = the fan is on

items.q: "You pick chocolate or vanilla, but not both."
items.why: "Or … but not both" = exactly one.
items.letters: `c` = you pick chocolate · `v` = you pick vanilla

items.q: "You log in only if the password and the 2FA code are right."
items.why: Main joiner *only if*: everything after it goes right.
items.letters: `l` = you log in · `p` = the password is right · `c` = the 2FA code is right

items.q: "Users see an error if the website or the payment gateway is down."
items.why: *If* in the middle → the part after it goes left (🔄).
items.letters: `w` = the website is up · `g` = the payment gateway is up · `e` = users see an error

items.q: "The café serves breakfast unless it's Sunday or it's after 11am."
items.a: `¬(s ∨ e) ⇒ b`, which is `(¬s ∧ ¬e) ⇒ b`, which is `b ∨ s ∨ e`
items.why: Unless = if not, applied to the whole "Sunday or after 11am".
items.letters: `b` = the café serves breakfast · `s` = it's Sunday · `e` = it's after 11am

items.q: Rewrite `¬(a ∨ ¬b)` with no `¬` in front of a bracket.
items.why: De Morgan, then `¬¬b` = `b`.

items.q: "The fire alarm rings exactly when there's smoke or someone presses test."
items.why: *Exactly when* = `⇔`.
items.letters: `f` = the fire alarm rings · `s` = there's smoke · `t` = someone presses test

items.q: Is `(p ∨ q) ⇒ r` the same as `(p ⇒ r) ∧ (q ⇒ r)`?
items.why: "If p or q, then r" = "p forces r, and q forces r".

items.q: "If the train is late, I take the bus unless I walk."
items.why: Outer *if*, inner *unless*.
items.letters: `t` = the train is late · `b` = I take the bus · `w` = I walk

blocks.title: 🔴 Quiz level: Q3b style
blocks.sub: Translate the sentence, then pick **every** option that means the same. Recipe: ① translate ② rewrite everything into `¬ ∧ ∨` ③ compare, or hunt for one row where they differ.

items.q: "The alarm rings whenever the door opens." Which options mean the same?
items.why: "Whenever the door opens" is the if-part → `d ⇒ a`. (3) is the `¬A ∨ B` form and (5) the contrapositive. (2) and (4) both say `a ⇒ d`, the converse.
items.letters: `a` = the alarm rings · `d` = the door opens

items.q: "The tests pass only if the code compiles." Which options mean the same?
items.why: "Only if" never flips → `t ⇒ c`. (3) is the contrapositive and (4) the `¬A ∨ B` form. (1) is the converse trap.
items.letters: `c` = the code compiles · `t` = the tests pass

items.q: "The request fails unless the server is up." Which options mean the same?
items.why: "Fails" is `¬r`. Unless = if not → `¬s ⇒ ¬r`. Its contrapositive is `r ⇒ s`, which is `¬r ∨ s`. (5) is `s ⇒ r`: the wrong direction.
items.letters: `s` = the server is up · `r` = the request succeeds

items.q: "The light is on just in case the switch is up." Which options mean the same?
items.why: `l ⇔ w` = "both on or both off", which is (1). (3) is `(l ⇒ w) ∧ (w ⇒ l)` rewritten. (2) and (5) mean "exactly one" (xor), the opposite. (4) is only one direction.
items.letters: `l` = the light is on · `w` = the switch is up

items.q: **S1:** "Whenever the tank is empty, the pump is off unless the system is in manual mode." Which options match S1?
items.why: S1 = `e ⇒ (¬m ⇒ ¬p)` = `¬e ∨ m ∨ ¬p`, which is (1). (5) opens up to the same thing by exportation.
items.letters: `e` = the tank is empty · `p` = the pump is running · `m` = the system is in manual mode

items.q: **S2** (same letters): "The pump runs only if the tank is not empty." Which options match S2?
items.letters: `e` = the tank is empty · `p` = the pump is running · `m` = the system is in manual mode

items.q: **S1:** "The office is open only if it's not a holiday." Which options match S1?
items.why: `o ⇒ ¬h` = `¬o ∨ ¬h`. Its contrapositive is `h ⇒ ¬o`.
items.letters: `h` = it's a holiday · `o` = the office is open · `w` = I work from home

items.q: **S2** (same letters): "I work from home just in case the office is closed." Which options match S2?
items.why: `w ⇔ ¬o` is true when exactly one of `w`, `o` is true. (3) says it as "one way or the other", (6) as "at least one, but not both". (4) is `w ⇔ o`, the trap.
items.letters: `h` = it's a holiday · `o` = the office is open · `w` = I work from home

items.q: "You get a bonus if you hit your target, provided you're not late more than twice." Which options mean the same?
items.why: "Provided ¬l" is the outer if, and "if t" the inner one: `¬l ⇒ (t ⇒ b)` = `l ∨ ¬t ∨ b`. (2) and (5) open up to the same thing. (3) is the converse. (4) is `b ⇒ (t ∨ ¬l)`, also the wrong direction.
items.letters: `b` = you get a bonus · `t` = you hit your target · `l` = you're late more than twice

blocks.sub: Beyond the quiz: mid-term and exam territory.

items.q: "The order ships just in case the payment clears, unless there's fraud." Which options mean the same?
items.why: The comma makes *unless* apply to the whole sentence. Unless = if not: `¬f ⇒ (s ⇔ p)` = `f ∨ (s ⇔ p)`. (4) and (5) each keep only one half of the `⇔`. (3) reverses the arrow.
items.letters: `p` = the payment clears · `f` = there's fraud · `s` = the order ships

items.q: Show that `¬(p ⇒ (q ⇒ r))` = `p ∧ q ∧ ¬r`, and say what it means.
items.a: `p ⇒ (q ⇒ r)` = `(p ∧ q) ⇒ r`, and its negation is `p ∧ q ∧ ¬r`.
items.why: In words: "p and q both happened, but r didn't". That is the only way to break the promise.

items.q: A detective knows three things: "If Alice is guilty, so is Bob", "Bob is guilty only if Carol is", and "Carol is not guilty". Translate all three. Can Alice be guilty?
items.why: `¬c` together with `b ⇒ c` forces `¬b`. Then `a ⇒ b` forces `¬a`. This chain is a preview of L4 (arguments).
items.letters: `a` = Alice is guilty · `b` = Bob is guilty · `c` = Carol is guilty

items.q: Is `(p ⇒ q) ∧ (q ⇒ r)` the same as `p ⇒ r`?
items.a: **No.** Row `p = F, q = T, r = F`: the left is `T ∧ (T ⇒ F)` = F, the right is `F ⇒ F` = T.
items.why: The chain **gives** you `p ⇒ r` (it entails it), but `p ⇒ r` alone doesn't give back the chain. Entailment is L4.

items.q: "Writes succeed only if the disk isn't full, and an alert fires whenever the disk is full." Translate. If writes succeed, what does this rule tell you about the alert?
items.a: `(w ⇒ ¬d) ∧ (d ⇒ a)`. If writes succeed, the disk isn't full, so the rule says **nothing** about the alert.
items.why: With `d = F`, `d ⇒ a` is true whatever `a` is.
items.letters: `d` = the disk is full · `w` = writes succeed · `a` = an alert fires

items.q: "The service is up if and only if the primary is healthy or, failing that, a replica is healthy."
items.why: "Failing that" adds nothing logical. It just means "or else", so at least one healthy node is enough.
items.letters: `s` = the service is up · `p` = the primary is healthy · `r` = a replica is healthy

blocks.sub: Don't do these now. Come back in 2 days and answer from memory.

items.q: "Neither the cat nor the dog is hungry."
items.why: Not this AND not that.
items.letters: `c` = the cat is hungry · `d` = the dog is hungry

items.q: Add brackets: `¬p ∨ q ⇒ r`
items.why: `¬`, then `∨`, then `⇒`.

items.q: "You can enter only if you have a ticket and ID."
items.why: Everything after *only if* goes right.
items.letters: `e` = you can enter · `t` = you have a ticket · `i` = you have ID

items.q: Write `A ⇒ (B ⇒ C)` with a single arrow.
items.why: Exportation.

items.q: Is `¬(p ∨ q)` the same as `¬p ∨ ¬q`?
items.a: **No.** Row `p = T, q = F`: the left is F, the right is T.
items.why: `¬(p ∨ q)` = `¬p ∧ ¬q`. De Morgan swaps `∨` for `∧`.

blocks.summary: Come back in 2 days and answer from memory.

lines: and / but / although / yet → `∧`. or → `∨` (inclusive). neither–nor → `¬A ∧ ¬B`. not both → `¬(A ∧ B)`.
`¬` first, then `∧ ∨`, then `⇒ ⇔`. Bracket every mix of `∧` and `∨`.
Recipe: letters (positive versions) → main joiner → halves → brackets.
Nested: `A ⇒ (B ⇒ C)` = `(A ∧ B) ⇒ C`. Whenever A, C unless B = `(A ∧ ¬B) ⇒ C`.
Equivalent = same in every row. One disagreeing row = not equivalent.
